---
title: "Parsing time expressions"
subtitle: "Resolve dates only when the reference date is explicit"
description: "Learn how simple R rules handle dates, weekdays, times of day, and durations in workforce text."
categories: [entity enrichment, temporal parsing, workforce research]
---

The phrase `Apply by October 15` gives the coordinator a month and day but no
year. The deadline needs a year before the team can add it to a calendar.

A date parser converts a time expression into a sortable date. Some expressions
give complete dates, while others need a reference date. Other expressions do
not describe calendar dates.

::: {.callout-note}
Riverton dates and notices in this lesson are invented teaching examples.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- separate full dates from relative dates.
- use an explicit reference date rather than `Sys.Date()`.
- recognize durations and times of day as different kinds of time language.
- compare a small temporal parser with this page's expected answers.
- compare the rule output with spaCy entity labels.
:::

## State the reference date

The examples use the fixed reference date 2026-08-28, a Friday. A date that
changes daily would prevent comparison with fixed expected results. The lesson
therefore passes the date as a variable and never calls `Sys.Date()`.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(spacyr)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

reference_date <- as.Date("2026-08-28")

temporal_examples <- tibble(
  expr_id = sprintf("time-%02d", 1:11),
  text = c(
    sentences |>
      filter(sentence_id == "s028") |>
      pull(text),
    "Evening",
    "12-week",
    "Monday",
    "next Friday",
    "next Monday",
    "2026-10-15",
    "starts in the fall",
    "Classes begin on September 14",
    sentences |>
      filter(sentence_id == "s020") |>
      pull(text),
    sentences |>
      filter(sentence_id == "s011") |>
      pull(text)
  ),
  expected_category = c(
    "reference-date needed",
    "not resolvable",
    "not resolvable",
    "reference-date needed",
    "reference-date needed",
    "reference-date needed",
    "fully resolved",
    "not resolvable",
    "reference-date needed",
    "not resolvable",
    "not resolvable"
  ),
  expected_date = as.Date(c(
    "2026-10-15",
    NA,
    NA,
    "2026-08-31",
    "2026-09-04",
    "2026-09-07",
    "2026-10-15",
    NA,
    "2026-09-14",
    NA,
    NA
  ))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  temporal_examples,
  col.names = c("Expression ID", "Text", "Expected category", "Expected date"),
  caption = "Temporal examples with expected answers",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(c("readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "purrr", "stringr", "spacyr") %in% loadedNamespaces()))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(nrow(temporal_examples), 11L),
  identical(format(reference_date, "%A"), "Friday")
)
```

`October 15` needs the reference year. `Evening` is a time of day without a date.
`12-week` is a duration, not a point on the calendar.

## Write a small resolver

The resolver first searches for a full ISO date, such as `2026-10-15`, in
year-month-day order. It then searches for a month and day, followed by weekdays.
The shorthand `\(text)` means "for each text value, execute this small function."

```{r}
resolve_temporal <- function(text, reference_date) {
  lower_text <- str_to_lower(text)

  if (str_detect(text, "\\b\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}\\b")) {
    return(list(
      category = "fully resolved",
      date = as.Date(str_extract(text, "\\b\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}\\b"))
    ))
  }

  month_match <- str_match(
    text,
    "\\b(January|February|March|April|May|June|July|August|September|October|November|December)\\s+(\\d{1,2})\\b"
  )

  if (!is.na(month_match[1, 1])) {
    resolved <- as.Date(paste(
      format(reference_date, "%Y"),
      match(month_match[1, 2], month.name),
      month_match[1, 3],
      sep = "-"
    ))
    return(list(category = "reference-date needed", date = resolved))
  }

  weekday_names <- c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday")

  if (str_detect(lower_text, "next friday")) {
    target_day <- 6L
    current_day <- as.POSIXlt(reference_date)$wday + 1L
    days_forward <- ((target_day - current_day) %% 7L) + 7L
    return(list(category = "reference-date needed", date = reference_date + days_forward))
  }

  found_weekday <- weekday_names[str_detect(lower_text, str_to_lower(weekday_names))]

  if (length(found_weekday) > 0L) {
    target_day <- match(found_weekday[1], weekday_names)
    current_day <- as.POSIXlt(reference_date)$wday + 1L
    days_forward <- (target_day - current_day) %% 7L
    if (days_forward == 0L) {
      days_forward <- 7L
    }
    return(list(category = "reference-date needed", date = reference_date + days_forward))
  }

  list(category = "not resolvable", date = as.Date(NA))
}

parsed_temporal <- map(
  temporal_examples$text,
  \(text) resolve_temporal(text, reference_date)
)

temporal_results <- temporal_examples |>
  mutate(
    category = map_chr(parsed_temporal, "category"),
    resolved_date = as.Date(map_chr(parsed_temporal, \(item) as.character(item$date)))
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  temporal_results |>
    select(expr_id, text, category, resolved_date),
  col.names = c("Expression ID", "Text", "Parser category", "Resolved date"),
  caption = "Rule-based temporal parsing results",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(temporal_results$resolved_date[1], as.Date("2026-10-15")),
  identical(temporal_results$resolved_date[4], as.Date("2026-08-31")),
  is.na(temporal_results$resolved_date[2])
)
```

The resolver assigns `Monday` to the next Monday after the reference date.
Month-day phrases use the reference year. `next Friday` has a separate branch,
while other weekday names mean their next occurrence. These are policy choices.

A rollover rule, which advances the year, would be necessary after October 15.
The `next Monday` result shows that the general weekday branch misses a
distinction in the expected answers.

## Score the examples

The resolver and expected answers share an author, so the score below does not
give an estimate of parser accuracy. It compares the page's actual behavior with its
stated behavior.

```{r}
date_matches <- (is.na(temporal_results$resolved_date) & is.na(temporal_results$expected_date)) |
  (!is.na(temporal_results$resolved_date) &
    !is.na(temporal_results$expected_date) &
    temporal_results$resolved_date == temporal_results$expected_date)

category_counts <- tibble(
  category = c("fully resolved", "reference-date needed", "not resolvable")
) |>
  left_join(
    temporal_results |>
      count(category, name = "examples"),
    by = join_by(category)
  ) |>
  mutate(examples = coalesce(examples, 0L))

score_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c("category matches", "date matches"),
  examples = c(
    sum(temporal_results$category == temporal_results$expected_category),
    sum(date_matches)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  category_counts,
  col.names = c("Parser category", "Examples"),
  caption = "Temporal categories in the examples",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  score_summary,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Matching examples"),
  caption = "Agreement with this page's expected answers",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(category_counts$examples, c(1L, 5L, 5L)),
  identical(score_summary$examples, c(11L, 10L))
)
```

One example is fully resolved from the text alone. Five need the reference date.
Five are not resolvable as a single date. The `next Monday` row is the date
mismatch: the rule treats it like `Monday`, while this lesson's expected answer
uses the following week.

## Compare spaCy entity labels

spaCy gives spans of text entity labels such as `DATE` and `TIME`. The labels
are useful clues, not answers to the resolution problem.

```{r}
source("R/use-spacy.R")

pipeline <- use_project_spacy()
pipeline_version <- spacy_pipeline_version()

spacy_parsed <- spacy_parse(
  setNames(temporal_examples$text, temporal_examples$expr_id),
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE,
  entity = TRUE,
  dependency = TRUE,
  nounphrase = TRUE
)
spacy_entities <- entity_extract(spacy_parsed, type = "all")

spacy_checks <- spacy_entities |>
  filter(doc_id %in% c("time-01", "time-02", "time-03")) |>
  select(doc_id, entity, entity_type)

spacy_finalize()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    name = pipeline_version$name,
    version = pipeline_version$version,
    language = pipeline_version$lang,
    license = pipeline_version$license,
    spacy = pipeline_version$spacy
  ),
  col.names = c("Pipeline", "Version", "Language", "License", "spaCy"),
  caption = "spaCy pipeline used for the entity comparison",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  spacy_checks,
  col.names = c("Expression ID", "Entity text", "spaCy label"),
  caption = "spaCy DATE and TIME labels on selected examples",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(pipeline_version$version, "3.8.0"),
  identical(pipeline_version$license, "MIT"),
  identical(pipeline_version$spacy, "3.8.7"),
  identical(
    spacy_checks$entity_type,
    c("DATE", "TIME", "DATE")
  )
)
```

spaCy gives `October 15` the label `DATE`, `Evening` the label `TIME`, and `12-week` the label
`DATE`. The first expression still needs a year. spaCy's training scheme puts
periods in the `DATE` class, so it assigns that label to `12-week`. That
label is correct under the scheme but does not specify a calendar date.

## Temporal parsing in production

Temporal-span detection is only the first step, as spaCy's `DATE` label for
`October 15` shows. Full normalization requires a dedicated tool, such as
Meta's Duckling or Python's `dateparser`, rather than custom R branches.

These tools distinguish concepts that custom rules can combine incorrectly:

- **Document Creation Time (DCT) / Reference Time**: Relative expressions such as `next Friday` or `tomorrow` require an explicit reference date. The document creation time can provide that reference. Callers must supply the date, for example through `RELATIVE_BASE` in `dateparser`.
- **Granularity and representative ambiguity**: Granularity is the size of the time unit. `last month` could mean the previous calendar month or the last 30 days. A parser must separate span detection from normalization and record those assumptions.

## What to remember

- A temporal parser needs a stated reference date for relative expressions.
- Month-day dates need a same-year or rollover policy.
- Weekday phrases need more than one `next Friday` special case.
- Entity labels can find time language without resolving a date.

The lesson supplies 2026 as the reference year, so `Apply by October 15`
resolves to a date in 2026. `Evening` and `starts in the fall` still give
this parser no specific day.
